content.thinking:
I need to write this up without exposing actual figures, using placeholders instead. I'm working through the causal chain: shopper monthly totals didn't reconcile with the underlying purchases, with some mismatched count out of a total, a widest discrepancy, and an oldest affected purchase, all tied back to specific evidence labels I need to cite.

The likely cause is that record_purchase stopped maintaining the running monthly total field after a particular deploy, since the onset timing lines up closely with that deploy — though this is the investigator's hypothesis and remains unverified, so I should flag it as an assumption rather than a confirmed fact. No automated check caught the regression at deploy time, and it was only found later through a periodic integrity check, with no error rate anomalies to have flagged it sooner. I should note the replica start times don't seem relevant here, and add new action items around repairing the already-corrupted records by recalculating totals from the underlying purchase data, in addition to the existing action items.

I'm organizing the new action items by type: AI-3 to repair damaged totals (mitigate), AI-4 to add an invariant test in CI (prevent), AI-5 to run the spend-integrity check more frequently with drift alerts (detect), and AI-6 to make the check runnable on-demand so Argus can verify rollback actions going forward (process). I'm mapping each contributing factor to its corresponding fix — the missing test/review ties to AI-4, the infrequent check ties to AI-5, the lack of a verification signal for rollback ties to AI-6 and AI-2, and the need to repair existing damaged records ties to AI-3, even though that one feels more like an impact than a root factor.

Now I'm thinking through how to phrase figures and durations using placeholders rather than concrete numbers, and planning out the executive summary and lessons-learned sections — noting what went well (accurate onset detection, quick fix draft), what went wrong (long undetected window, no error metric, no action taken on rollback), and what we got lucky on (the check eventually caught it, and the underlying purchase records were still intact so the total is recoverable).

action_items.item: Rewrite every affected shopper's stored monthly total from the purchases behind it, then re-run the spend-integrity check to confirm no totals are out of step.
Add an automated test that recording a purchase updates the shopper's monthly total, and run it before every deploy of this service.
Run the spend-integrity check far more often, or check each write, and page on the first drift instead of waiting for the periodic run.
Make the spend-integrity check runnable on demand, scoped to recent purchases, so Argus can verify a rollback worked and take it directly.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' stored spend totals did not reconcile with the purchases behind them: {A1} of {A2} totals were wrong, the widest short by {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase dated from {A4}. The service stayed up and the metrics showed no error rate, so this was silent wrong data.

The wrong totals begin at {began}, which is {began - P2.1} after deploy P2 went out at {P2.1}. The earlier deploy P1 predates the onset by hours. Every purchase recorded since the onset therefore left its shopper's total out of step.

Deploy P2 changed the purchase-recording code so it no longer maintains the shopper's monthly total when a purchase is written. This mechanism is the Investigator's inference and was not confirmed in logs or the diff. The fix is drafted in a pull request, but the totals already written are not repaired by it.

The release reached production without anything catching the broken total. The only check that compares totals with purchases runs every {A5} days, so the fault was found only at {alert_raised} and was up to that old. The record does not show why the release passed review and testing.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing in review or testing caught that recording a purchase no longer updated the shopper's total. The record does not show what tests exist for this path.
The only detection was a spend-integrity check that runs every {A5} days. The fault ran undetected for at least {duration}, and no latency or error series moved.
Argus could not confirm within its waiting time that a rollback had worked, so it recommended the rollback instead of taking it. The bad code stayed live while a person was found.
A rollback or a fix stops further damage but does not repair the totals already written wrongly, so the existing damage persists after mitigation.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers' stored spend totals stopped matching their purchases. The fault began at {began}. When the integrity check found it at {alert_raised}, {A1} of {A2} shopper totals were wrong, and the widest was short by {A3}. The service was still broken at the last minute of metrics read, so it was broken for at least {duration}, and that figure is a lower bound. Nothing slowed down or errored, so only the periodic integrity check, which runs every {A5} days, noticed. The timing points to a code release made just before the onset. Argus recognised this and recommended a rollback. It did not take the rollback itself, because it had no way to confirm within its waiting time that the rollback worked. It also drafted a fix as a pull request. Argus held the incident for {held}, and that measures the response, not the fault. A person still needs to roll back or merge the fix, and the totals already written wrongly need repairing separately.

got_lucky: The fault corrupted derived totals without any error or outage. Argus's account does not say the purchases themselves were lost, so the totals can likely be rebuilt. That was luck, not a safeguard.
went_well: Argus placed the onset at {began}, one step after deploy P2, and named the deploy as the leading candidate within {held}.
A draft fix pull request was ready soon after the incident was handed to a person.
went_wrong: The fault went undetected for at least {duration} because only a periodic check could see it.
Argus read no logs, so the mechanism of the fault is unconfirmed.
No metrics from before the onset were available, so no error rate could be compared.
No mitigation was taken automatically, so the incident ended with the faulty release still live and the damage unrepaired.

input.root_cause: The deploy at {P2.1} changed the purchase-recording path so that it stopped keeping each shopper's running monthly total up to date. Every purchase recorded afterwards left the stored total out of step with the purchases behind it. The service stayed fast and error-free, so nothing flagged it. The code-level mechanism comes from the Investigator's account. Argus did not read logs or the diff to confirm it.
